title: Where the adjective goes
description: Say what something is like, in the right order.
grammarNote: An adjective usually goes after the noun: un coche rojo. Some go before, and then they are more literary.

explanation.summary: In everyday Spanish the adjective comes after the noun. A few adjectives go before it, and they then carry a different feel, usually more literary or more emphatic.

sections.heading: After, or before
sections.body: The usual order is noun then adjective: un problema grave, una casa pequeña. A small set of adjectives go before the noun, and they are the ones that are more literary or more emphatic: un gran hombre, las buenas intenciones, el propio médico. The verb ser is what tells you which is which: un gran hombre is a great man, and un hombre grande is a big man.

sections.heading: Two adjectives together
sections.body: When two adjectives describe the same noun, they normally come after it and are joined by y: un informe largo y detallado. But there is one exception: a colour goes straight after the noun and the other adjective follows: un abrigo azul oscuro. A noun that names a material goes after the adjective: un reloj de oro.

examples.es: Es un informe largo y detallado.
examples.en: It is a long and detailed report.
examples.note: Two adjectives joined by y, after the noun.

examples.en: He has a dark blue coat.
examples.note: A colour comes first of the two.
A material goes after the adjective.

items.note: Grande goes after the noun. Gran goes before it.
Pequeño goes after the noun. Pequeño is the same in both positions.
Excelente goes before the noun, usually.
A colour goes straight after the noun.
Claro goes after the noun. Claro also means of course.
Propio goes before the noun: mi propio hijo.
Mismo goes after the noun: la misma razón.
